results.summary: In pooled analyses, the MoCA demonstrated significantly higher sensitivity for detecting mild cognitive impairment compared to the MMSE (pooled sensitivity 0.89 vs 0.59 for MCI). The MMSE's ceiling effect is particularly pronounced in individuals with higher educational attainment, who may score in the normal range despite objective cognitive decline detectable on more sensitive instruments.
results.title: Sensitivity of the MoCA and MMSE for detection of MCI: a systematic review and meta-analysis

results.summary: The 2018 AAN guideline recommends neuropsychological testing and brief structured cognitive batteries for evaluation of MCI. The guideline notes that the MMSE may be insensitive for early cognitive changes, particularly in persons with high premorbid intelligence or education, and recommends more comprehensive evaluation when clinical concern persists despite normal screening scores.
results.title: AAN Practice Guideline Update: Mild cognitive impairment

results.summary: The ATN framework classifies Alzheimer pathology by biomarker: A (amyloid, positive amyloid PET or reduced CSF Abeta42/40 ratio), T (tau, elevated CSF p-tau or tau PET), N (neurodegeneration, hippocampal atrophy or FDG hypometabolism). Individuals meeting A+T+ criteria are classified as having Alzheimer's disease regardless of clinical stage, including MCI.
results.title: NIA-AA Research Framework: Toward a biological definition of Alzheimer's disease

output.summary: The MoCA is substantially more sensitive than the MMSE for detecting mild cognitive impairment, particularly in individuals with higher educational or occupational attainment where ceiling effects limit the MMSE's discriminant ability. The AAN 2018 guideline supports comprehensive neuropsychological evaluation when clinical concern persists despite normal brief screening scores. The NIA-AA 2018 ATN framework provides a biomarker-based classification scheme for Alzheimer pathology that can confirm diagnosis at the MCI stage.

key_clinical_evidence: The MMSE has a well-documented ceiling effect, particularly in individuals with higher premorbid education and occupational attainment; a score of 28/30 does not exclude early MCI-AD and should not terminate the workup when informant-reported functional change is present

The MoCA is substantially more sensitive than the MMSE for detecting mild cognitive impairment; a MoCA score of 21/30 in the setting of a normal MMSE 28/30 is the core diagnostic tension in this case and must be resolved in favor of the more sensitive instrument

The neuropsychological profile — storage-type episodic memory deficit (RAVLT delayed recall at the 6th percentile with poor cueing benefit), mild anomia, and semantic fluency reduction — is the hallmark amnestic pattern of MCI due to Alzheimer's disease
The case-designated optional CSF Aβ42/40 and phospho-tau profile can support Alzheimer pathology when biological confirmation would change management; amyloid PET is not duplicated

Mild Fazekas grade 1 small vessel disease and controlled vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension) are common comorbidities in this age group but are insufficient to account for the amnestic profile and do not argue against an Alzheimer diagnosis

Cultural and language considerations in Hispanic bilingual patients may affect test performance on language-dominant subtests; the use of normed instruments and clinical context is essential to avoid over- or under-diagnosing cognitive impairment

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Elena Vargas is a 69-year-old right-handed bilingual retired elementary school teacher who presents to the outpatient neurology clinic accompanied by her husband, Roberto, for evaluation of gradually worsening memory and word-finding concerns. Her husband first became aware of the changes approximately ten months ago when he noticed she had begun repeating questions during conversations that had occurred earlier the same day — asking twice, for example, whether their daughter was planning to call that evening. Initially he attributed this to fatigue or stress. Over subsequent months, he observed that she sometimes forgot appointments that had been clearly discussed and entered in her phone calendar, something he says was uncharacteristic of a woman who had spent decades organizing an elementary school classroom. On three occasions she mislaid her reading glasses and spent considerable time searching for them before finding them in unusual places. Her husband noticed that her grocery shopping has become less reliable; she occasionally returns home without items on a written list she carried with her. He also reports that she has become noticeably slower at reading Spanish-language novels, stopping more frequently and sometimes re-reading the same paragraph — she herself has commented that 'the words don't stick.' She continues to manage household finances, drive on familiar routes without incident, prepare meals, and care for herself independently in all activities of daily living including bathing, dressing, and medication management. Her daughters have not observed any personality change or mood disturbance beyond mild frustration when she notices a memory lapse. She denies persistent sadness, tearfulness, anhedonia, or neurovegetative symptoms of depression. Sleep is described as restorative by both herself and her husband; there are no reports of acting out dreams, excessive daytime sleepiness, or witnessed apneic episodes. She denies hallucinations, paranoid ideation, or behavioral changes. There have been no falls, seizures, tremor, or incontinence. Her appetite is unchanged and her weight has been stable. She was seen by her primary care physician six weeks ago, who administered an MMSE that scored 28/30. The physician reassured her and her husband that the score was in the normal range, but given the persistence of the complaints and the informant report, referred her to neurology. Mrs. Vargas herself says 'I know something is off — I was never like this with my students.'
